 Foreword
The Government of Kenya is committed to providing quality education as a basic human right for all
Kenyans in line with regional and international obligations. While efforts have been made to expand
educational access, the government’s ambition is to ensure that all citizens receive quality education.
The government has invested heavily in the provision of educational materials,infrastructure, and
human resources in order to enhance the quality of education delivered in Kenyan schools. The
evidence-based interventions and global best practices have been adopted in teaching early grade
literacy programmes.
The basis of the ongoing education reform is to make education in Kenya competitive internationally and
socio-economically viable. The government is ensuring that education strives to stimulate innovation
and enhance acquisition of 21st Century skills. These are embedded in the competencies,pertinent and
contemporary issues as well as the values in the reformed curriculum.
Tusome instructional materials have been developed to enhance literacy competencies which are
the foundational skills for quality education. This book will guide learning and teaching in Grade 3
aligned to the Competence Based Curriculum. The design of the book has taken into consideration
evidence-based strategies for developing literacy skills and will ensure that learners acquire skills that
are relevant to their level. I would like to urge partners, teachers and other stakeholders to continue
supporting the reforms in the education sector for improved learning outcomes.
Ambassador (Dr.) Amina C. Mohamed, EGH, CAV
Cabinet Secretary,
Ministry of Education
 Preface
The Ministry of Education is committed to providing quality education to all learners as stipulated
in the Constitution of Kenya, 2010. The Competence Based Curriculum in education is intended to
address performance indicators of quality education. Research initiatives including the National
Assessment Monitoring Learning Achievement (NASMLA) and the Southern and East Africa Consortium
for Monitoring Education Quality (SACMEQ) highlighted gaps that need to be addressed in improving
learning outcomes.
Recent developments in the education reform process emphasize the role of literacy and numeracy
competencies in supporting learning, especially in the foundational early grades. The increasing focus
on the quality of education has resulted in interventions that have shown a positive impact on literacy
and numeracy outcomes. The Tusome National Literacy Program has improved literacy outcomes in
Grades 1 & 2, necessitating the expansion of the programme to Grade 3.
This book has been developed to support teaching of English in Grade 3 aligned to the Competence Based
Curriculum. It focuses on innovative teaching and learning approaches and also includes pertinent and
emerging issues.
The Ministry of Education appreciates the financial support provided by USAID. I also wish to thank
other partners and stakeholders for their contributions towards development and production of these
books.
Dr. Belio R. Kipsang, CBS
Principal Secretary
State Department of Early Learning and Basic Education
Ministry of Education
 Guide to the teacher
This Teacher’s Guide is based on the Direct Instruction approach. The approach helps teachers
to instruct learners in the fundamental skills that are necessary for improving fluency in reading,
comprehension and writing. The approach allows for a gradual release of responsibility of the
skill being taught using three simple steps; model, guided practice, and independent practice
or assessment. The teacher, in this approach, utilizes a more balanced teaching strategy
and presents a more diverse set of activities within classrooms. While the approach gives
room for the teacher’s creativity, teacher preparation still remains key to the success of the
lesson in this guide. The teacher is encouraged to devise and use relevant and contextually
applicable teaching and learning resources that will enhance mastery of the content taught.
Such resources may include, but not limited to, a dictionary, murals and realia.
While blackboard usage is important and encouraged in this guide, the approach lays emphasis
on a learner having their own individual text book to increase exposure to the text. In addition,
there are exercises in the Pupil’s Book that the learner needs to practice independently. These
exercises can be used during classwork or as extended homework. Homework is provided in
the lesson guide. The teacher needs to refer the learner to do these activities at home. This is
aimed at ensuring guardian or parental participation. The teacher is encouraged to find time
to check the learner’s work to ensure the activities are done and formative feedback is given in
a timely manner. It is also good to note that the teacher should not feel limited to only assign
these homework activities. If the learner requires more practice in a specific skill, the teacher
should use his/ her judgment to assign appropriate homework activities.
The teacher is also encouraged to choose the most appropriate activity that will make the
learner understand the concept taught. Such activities include use of pictures, demonstrations,
role play or explanations using words that are familiar, simple and short.
This Teacher’s Guide has been designed in a way that removes barriers to learning for all
learners regardless of their abilities or impairments. Learning impairments include mild to
moderately severe challenges. Such learners may be (and have always been) supported by
their teachers in several ways. The following are various ways that a teacher can support a
learner with various learning impairments:
Hearing impaired: Let the learner sit near the teacher. The teacher should identify and use
relevant realia or pictorials as teaching and learning materials.
Visually impaired: Let the learner sit either near or far from the board depending on where
they can see well. Avoid visual disruptors such as reflective mirrors in the classroom. Identify
and use relevant realia or pictorials as teaching and learning materials.
Learning difficulties: Set aside more time for remedial teaching. Teach at a slower pace and
encourage the learner no matter how small the effort they make.
Speech disorder: Be patient with the child and give them more time to complete their sentences.
Formatively, encourage the learner in their efforts however little.
Gifted and talented: Give the pupil additional or more challenging tasks to stimulate their
brain. Give the learner an opportunity for their talent to grow.
If any of the suggested ways do not work, the teacher is encouraged to refer the child for
further professional help.
